bib.title: Standards of coding and creating maintainable ML code (Chapter 10, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: Which common coding mistakes make ML code bases unstable and hard to maintain, and how are they fixed?
contributions: Table of common code smells in ML code
Five 'deadly' practices with fixes: poor naming/structure/architecture, tuple unpacking, blind try/catch, global mutable objects, excessively nested logic

limits: No data or measurement: all evidence is the author's experience and small synthetic Python examples.
Author concedes the topics are not exhaustive.
Code uses sklearn mean_squared_error(squared=False), later deprecated in scikit-learn in favour of root_mean_squared_error (dated; this is a note from the reader, not stated in the text).
Text says dictionary approach needs 32,768 conditions for 8 models, inconsistent with 5 buckets (5**8 = 390,625).
The 'Python hash table limit of 226' is an extraction loss of a superscript (likely 2^26 = 67,108,864).
practices: Avoid wildcard imports, too many parameters, copied boilerplate for train/test/inference feature code, untuned default hyperparameters outside prototyping, variable reuse, magic literals (use named constants), explanatory in-line comments, SQL without CTEs, and constant recasting (Table 10.1, p270-271).
Name variables descriptively and never reuse reserved/built-in names such as tuple or return-like names (10.2.1, p273-274).
Do not write dense one-liners; use descriptive intermediate variables and use library functions (sklearn mean_squared_error) rather than reimplementing (10.2.2, p274-276).
Pass hardcoded values in via configuration rather than inside functions (Listing 10.4 callout, p275).
Put large, isolated or many-class-touching new functionality in a new module rather than shoehorning it into an existing class; remove replaced code instead of commenting it out (10.2.3, p276-278).
Return named tuples (Scala case class analogue) instead of positional or nested tuples so return structure can change without editing callers (10.3.2, p280-282).
Catch specific exceptions, never blind except/pass; log with time, exception type, values and function name, and re-raise when the input is invalid (10.4, p283-288).
Add post-condition checks, such as input length equals output length, raising a custom exception (Listing 10.13, p287).
Log to a central, parseable place such as a logging service or MLflow instead of print (p285-286). 'When in doubt, log it out.' (p288).
Avoid mutable default arguments; default to None and create a new object (10.5.2, p290-291).
Use encapsulation so a function depends only on its arguments and exposes only its return value, which makes it testable (p291).
Replace deep if/elif/else trees and giant lookup dictionaries with computed mappings that scale to more inputs (10.6, p292-297).
If you find yourself copying and pasting large blocks of logic, stop and rethink the design (p296).

terms.definition: Indicators within the code (a term famously coined by Martin Fowler) of potentially crippling problems elsewhere, affecting production stability or debuggability.
Control flow in the code organized as well as noodles in a bowl of spaghetti.
A morass of individual bowls of spaghetti with duplicated code, global references, dead code, and no seeming architectural design for maintainability.
Changes need to be identically matched in all places, e.g. feature-engineering code for training, test and inference defined in three places.
A misguided intention to 'just make it work' by the inappropriate use of a try/catch block.
A bug that seemingly disappears when you try to investigate it.
A bug so complex and nondeterministic that it seems as complex as a fractal.
Restricting end-user access to internal functionality, and enforcing execution of logic on a bundle of the data passed in and the logic in the method.
